name: Binary Fuse Filter (binfuse C++ library)
workload: Static approximate-membership filter construction/query over up to 10 billion 64-bit keys; storage overhead measured against the information-theoretic lower bound
claimed_speedup: Binary fuse filters are within 13% of the storage lower bound vs 23% for xor filters and 44% for Bloom filters, without sacrificing query speed (paper, arXiv:2201.01174); binfuse's own sharded_filter benchmark measured populate ~48-93 ns/key and query ~46-53 ns/key at 100M-1B keys
compiler_and_flags: gcc-13 / clang-18 in CI matrix; binfuse_bench built with -DBINFUSE_BENCH=ON, no optimization flags stated for that specific run
tradeoffs: Filter is immutable once populated (no incremental inserts); populate needs significant RAM unless using sharded_filter; sharding needed for datasets beyond a few hundred million keys on commodity RAM
caveats: The underlying reference C implementation (FastFilter/xor_singleheader) is already on the known/catalogued list; binfuse is a distinct C++ wrapper + mmap-based sharding layer around it. The headline 13%/23%/44% overhead figures come from the original paper, not a re-measured head-to-head table in this repo's own README.
found_via: arXiv API search all:binary OR fuse OR filter -> arXiv:2201.01174 'Binary Fuse Filters: Fast and Smaller Than Xor Filters'; gh search repos "binary fuse filter"

name: Ribbon Filter (ribbonGo)
workload: Static approximate-membership filter over n=1e6 and n=1e8 keys, r=7 result bits, following the Dillinger & Walzer (2021) evaluation methodology
claimed_speedup: w=128 at n=1e6 achieves 7.334 bits/key (4.7% over the 7-bit information-theoretic minimum) vs Bloom's 9.6 bits/key at the same FPR - a 23.6% space saving; build 106.3 ns/key, query 43.2/31.7 ns/op (positive/negative) at n=1e6
compiler_and_flags: go test -bench, Go >=1.24; exact compiler build flags/version for the measured run not pinned in the README
hardware: Build/Space tables measured on an Apple M3 Pro (ARM64); Query table re-measured on a separate x86 Xeon Platinum host, so absolute ns/op is not comparable across build vs query tables
tradeoffs: Static/immutable once built (no incremental insert), no deletion support, construction cost is higher than Bloom's simple incremental build
caveats: Third-party Go reimplementation of the original C++ ribbon filter paper (arXiv:2103.02515), not the paper authors' own repo; build and query figures were measured on two different physical hosts.
found_via: arXiv API search all:ribbon OR filter OR approximate OR membership -> arXiv:2103.02515 'Ribbon filter: practically smaller than Bloom and Xor'; gh search repos "ribbon filter"

name: Bumped Ribbon Retrieval (BuRR) / homogeneous ribbon filter
workload: Static AMQ / retrieval data structure benchmark on synthetic key sets, measuring space overhead and construction/query throughput against Bloom, Cuckoo, and Xor filters
claimed_speedup: BuRR achieves space overhead well below 1% vs Bloom filter's >=44% overhead and is described as faster than classical Bloom filters; the faster ribbon variants are only moderately slower than Bloom/Xor in query while having at least an order of magnitude smaller space overhead
hardware: AMD EPYC 7702, 64 cores, 2.0GHz base / 3.35GHz boost, 1TiB DDR4-3200, Ubuntu 20.04
tradeoffs: Static/immutable; construction is a banded linear-algebra solve rather than simple hashing, which is more complex to implement/port than Bloom hashing
caveats: lorenzhs/burr is already on the known-catalogued list; included here only as additional Tier A evidence per the assignment's exception rule, since the paper provides a fully reproducible benchmark (public code, stated compiler/flags/hardware) directly targeting the Bloom/Cuckoo/Xor baselines.
found_via: arXiv API search all:ribbon OR filter OR approximate OR membership -> arXiv:2109.01892 'Fast Succinct Retrieval and Approximate Membership using Ribbon'

name: Cuckoo-GPU
workload: Batch insert/query/delete of 4M (L2-resident) and 268M (DRAM-resident) items at 95% load factor with 16-bit fingerprints, vs a CPU Partitioned Cuckoo Filter (PCF) and other GPU AMQ baselines (TCF, GQF, Blocked Bloom, BCHT)
claimed_speedup: vs CPU Partitioned Cuckoo Filter (PCF): 175x faster insert / 351x faster query (L2-resident, 4M items) and 69x / 143x faster (DRAM-resident, 268M items); also up to 378x faster insert, 6x faster query, 258x faster delete than GPU Counting Quotient Filter (GQF), and up to 108x faster delete than GPU Two-Choice Filter (TCF)
hardware: NVIDIA GH200 (H100 HBM3, 3.4 TB/s) for Cuckoo-GPU and GPU baselines; Intel Xeon W9-3595X CPU (120 threads) for the CPU Partitioned Cuckoo Filter comparison
tradeoffs: Requires a CUDA-capable NVIDIA GPU vs a CPU-only cuckoo filter; deliberately sacrifices cache locality to saturate GPU memory bandwidth, which would be a poor strategy on CPU
caveats: Companion code for a 2026 paper (arXiv:2603.15486, DOI 10.1145/3832810.3832822); the CPU-vs-GPU comparisons mix hardware generations (GH200 vs Xeon W9-3595X), so part of the speedup reflects the hardware jump, not only the algorithm; on GPU-vs-GPU insert against the append-only Blocked Bloom filter it is actually 0.35x (slower).
found_via: arXiv API search all:cuckoo OR filter -> arXiv:2603.15486 'Cuckoo-GPU: Accelerating Cuckoo Filters on Modern GPUs'; gh search repos "cuckoo-gpu"

name: Windowed Cuckoo Filter (WindowFilter, implements 'Smaller and More Flexible Cuckoo Filters')
workload: Bit-packed Bloom filter, standard Cuckoo(2,4) filter, and overlapping-window Cuckoo(2,2) filter compared on bytes/item, false-positive rate, lookup/insert latency, and max load factor
claimed_speedup: Windowed cuckoo (2,2): 1.5958 bytes/item vs Bloom's 1.8034 (~12% less memory) and vs Cuckoo(2,4)'s 2.1299 (~25% less memory); also the fastest lookup at 60.28 ns vs Bloom's 81.59 ns and Cuckoo's 61.19 ns
tradeoffs: Insert is slower than both Bloom and plain Cuckoo (162.97 ns vs 93.61 / 58.74 ns) because of the overlapping-window relocation logic
caveats: Third-party Rust reimplementation of arXiv:2505.05847 (Smaller and More Flexible Cuckoo Filters), not the paper authors' own code; 0 stars, brand-new (pushed 2026-09-03); no CPU/hardware model or compiler flags stated for the benchmark table, and it is the project's own benchmark, so capped at Tier C.
found_via: arXiv API search all:quotient OR filter -> arXiv:2505.05847 'Smaller and More Flexible Cuckoo Filters'; gh search repos "windowed cuckoo filter"

name: ChainedFilter
workload: RocksDB point-query tail latency with ChainedFilter's chain-rule membership filter versus RocksDB's stock Bloom filter; also external-memory accesses for Cuckoo Hashing and static-dictionary space overhead
claimed_speedup: reduces up to 36% of P99 tail point-query latency in RocksDB (which relies on Bloom filters for point lookups); reduces up to 31% external memory accesses for Cuckoo Hashing; needs only 26% extra space over the theoretical lower bound for an implicit static dictionary and only 0.22 extra bits/item for lossless data compression
tradeoffs: A general 'chain rule' framework composing several elementary filters rather than a drop-in single filter; the RocksDB integration is a case study, not a merged patch to upstream RocksDB
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo, so the code is all-rights-reserved by default and must be treated as reference/study-only; the repo says the code is provided to help understand the paper's algorithms, not as a packaged library; CPU/hardware model for the reported percentages is not stated.
found_via: arXiv API search all:approximate OR membership OR query OR filter -> arXiv:2308.13632 'ChainedFilter: Combining Membership Filters by Chain Rule'; gh search repos "chainedfilter"

name: Adaptive Learned Bloom Filter (Ada-BF)
workload: False-positive rate vs. memory budget on a malicious-URL dataset (485,730 URLs, 16.47% malicious) and other real-world datasets; standard Bloom filter vs. learned Bloom filter (LBF), sandwiched LBF, Ada-BF, and disjoint Ada-BF
claimed_speedup: Ada-BF/disjoint Ada-BF reduce overall FPR by over 80% and save over 50% memory vs. prior learned Bloom filter approaches at matched size; at filter size=500Kb, Ada-BF reduces FPR by 81% vs LBF/sandwiched LBF (disjoint: 84%); to hit FPR~=0.35%, Ada-BF cuts required memory from >500Kb (LBF) to 300Kb (>40% memory savings)
tradeoffs: Requires training/maintaining a classifier model alongside the filter; memory savings depend on how well the model's score distribution separates keys from non-keys, so gains are dataset-dependent
caveats: Reference Python research code with no LICENSE file (reference/study-only); this is a numerical FPR/memory comparison, not a systems-level speed benchmark, so no CPU/hardware or compiler details apply.
found_via: arXiv API search all:learned OR bloom OR filter -> arXiv:1910.09131 'Adaptive Learned Bloom Filter (Ada-BF): Efficient Utilization of the Classifier'; gh search repos "Ada-BF"

name: Partitioned Learned Bloom Filter (PLBF)
workload: False-positive rate vs. space tradeoff on a synthetic dataset, a URL dataset, and the EMBER malware dataset, comparing PLBF against a theoretically-optimal Bloom filter, sandwiched learned Bloom filter, and Ada-BF
claimed_speedup: at matched space (400Kb/500Kb/3000Kb for synthetic/URLs/EMBER), PLBF achieves 22x, 26x, and 3x smaller false-positive rates than the sandwiching approach, and 8.5x, 9x, 1.9x smaller than Ada-BF; to hit FPR=0.001, sandwiching needs 8.8x/3.3x/1.2x the space of PLBF and Ada-BF needs 6x/2.5x/1.1x the space
tradeoffs: Needs a trained scoring model plus a dynamic-program solve for optimal partition thresholds; benefit shrinks when the model is weak (EMBER dataset shows only a slight improvement)
caveats: ICLR 2020 peer-reviewed paper; repo is research code with no LICENSE file (reference/study-only); the headline multipliers are against Ada-BF and sandwiched LBF, not a raw standard-Bloom-filter number, though an 'optimal Bloom filter' curve is also plotted in the paper as the ultimate reference line.
found_via: arXiv API search all:learned OR bloom OR filter -> arXiv:2006.03176 'Partitioned Learned Bloom Filter'; gh search repos "partitioned learned bloom filter"

name: Cascaded Learned Bloom Filter (CLBF)
workload: False-positive-rate-vs-memory tradeoff on real-world datasets, comparing CLBF (a unified framework generalizing Sandwiched LBF and Partitioned LBF with a dynamic-programming size optimizer) against PLBF and Sandwiched LBF at matched target FPR
claimed_speedup: at the same target FPR (e.g. F=0.005), CLBF reduces memory usage by up to 17% compared to PLBF, the strongest prior learned-Bloom-filter baseline in their tests
tradeoffs: Adds a DP-based size/threshold optimizer at construction time (paper reports this is 0.3-24% of total build time); like other learned filters, needs a trained scoring model and benefits are dataset/model dependent
caveats: No public code repository was found for CLBF itself (checked GitHub search); the paper's own optimized C++ reimplementation used for benchmarking is not released, so this is has_code=false / no-code Tier C even though it is a rigorous, quantified comparison against PLBF and Sandwiched LBF.
found_via: arXiv API search all:learned OR bloom OR filter -> arXiv:2502.03696 'Cascaded Learned Bloom Filter for Optimizing Model-Filter Size Balance and Fast Rejection'
